sources.design: Systematic review of 30 studies and 614 patients; no level I/II comparative studies.
sources.population: 114 tendinopathies and 500 partial tears; diagnosis and treatment selection heterogeneous.
sources.coInterventions: Activity modification, immobilization, strengthening variably reported
sources.outcomes: Both strategies described improvement; heterogeneous low-level evidence prevents pooling/equivalence inference.
sources.followUp: Study-specific; synthesis reports median follow-up of 24 months.
sources.uncertainty: Selected indexed abstract/discussion/tables inspected, not complete article; do not apply partial-tear escalation to isolated tendinopathy.
sources.harms: No isolated-tendinopathy loading harm/risk estimate established.
sources.limitations: 30 studies/614 patients: 114 tendinopathies and 500 partial tears; no level I/II comparative studies, so no meta-analysis. Both operative and nonoperative reports describe pain/function improvement, but selection strongly favors nonoperative care for tendinopathy and surgery for tears. Conservative care varies (activity modification, immobilization, strengthening); dose reporting is poor. These mixed-pathology results cannot establish a loading protocol or rupture risk for isolated tendinopathy. Tendinopathy/partial tear/complete rupture and postoperative rehabilitation must remain distinct. Low-level literature and heterogeneity, rather than evidence of equivalence, constrain comparisons.

sources.population: 19-year-old male collegiate pitcher, suspected distal biceps tendinopathy, symptoms6 weeks; no imaging confirmation
sources.coInterventions: Manual therapy, ROM, forearm stretching, later concentric/plyometric sport work
sources.outcomes: Pain/function/strength improved; returned to offseason pitching; component efficacy cannot be isolated.
sources.followUp: Five visits over4 weeks; short-term follow-up
sources.uncertainty: Single athlete, unconfirmed diagnosis; narrative3×7 versus first-table3×10 discrepancy; not safe generic heavy loading.
sources.limitations: One 19-year-old baseball pitcher with suspected distal biceps tendinopathy, symptoms 6 weeks, five visits over 4 weeks. Pain-free ROM, manual therapy, forearm stretching and eccentric loading progressed to concentric and sport-specific plyometrics. Narrative prescribes eccentric 3×7, daily after visit two, controlled 3-second lowering; first-visit table instead lists 3×10 with 3-lb dumbbell. Stretch 3×30 seconds; later concentric 3×10. This case-specific/table discrepancy precludes one canonical dose. Improved pain/function/strength and returned to offseason pitching; no comparator and diagnosis not imaging-confirmed. Avoiding provoking heavy lifting, power cleans and pitching was individualized treatment advice, not tested universal contraindications. Harms not systematically established.

protocol.execution: Initially low-load eccentric elbow-flexor lowering in midrange, multiple forearm grips; Figure1 describes contralateral-arm assistance with dumbbell neutral/supinated and pulley variants. Later concentric and plyometric progressions are distinct.
protocol.dose: Narrative: eccentric 3×7. Initial table: 3×10 with 3-lb dumbbell. Later concentric: 3×10. Forearm/biceps stretch: 3×30 seconds. Preserve discrepancy.
protocol.frequency: Daily gym eccentric work after second visit, as individually instructed.
protocol.supervision: Five physical-therapy visits over4 weeks; home/gym exercise.
protocol.progression: Individual pain/function/strength-guided progression; later resisted/provocative tests asymptomatic before plyometrics. No transferable universal loading algorithm.
protocol.stoppingRules: Avoid individually provoking heavy lifting/power cleans/pitching initially; narrative tolerability wording was case-specific, not a validated pain threshold.

sources.population: 12 tendinopathies and 9 partial tears; complete ruptures excluded.
sources.coInterventions: Three-week supinated long-arm splint, NSAIDs and physical therapy; refractory cases received injection or surgery.
sources.outcomes: Five continued failures undergoing surgery had partial tears; no isolated exercise effect.
sources.followUp: not fully established in inspected passages
sources.uncertainty: Only indexed selected passages/primary metadata inspected; complete publisher PDF403. Splint position not a workout angle.
sources.limitations: 21 patients, 12 tendinopathy and 9 partial tears. Complete ruptures were excluded and managed surgically. Initial care included a long-arm splint in forearm supination for 3 weeks, NSAIDs/physical therapy; refractory cases proceeded to ultrasound-guided injection and, for five continued failures with partial tears, surgery. No exercise-versus-control test or isolated exercise dose. Splint position is an initial treatment exposure, not a safe workout ROM threshold. Mixed pathology and escalation confound attribution; report cannot prove which movements cause rupture.
